strings.hist.soviet.order_270.title: Order No. 270: captivity as treason
strings.hist.soviet.order_270.text: On 16 August 1941 Stalin, Molotov, Army General Zhukov and four marshals signed Order No. 270 of the Soviet High Command. Commanders and political officers who surrendered in battle counted as malicious deserters: they were to be shot on the spot and their families arrested. Families of captured Red Army soldiers lost state support. The order was read out in every company but published only in 1988. Of up to 5.7 million Red Army soldiers in German captivity, around three million died. Those who survived and came home remained suspect. A secret resolution of 29 June 1956 admitted “gross violations of the law”; only a decree of 24 January 1995 called the persecution politically motivated.
strings.hist.soviet.special_settlements.title: Special settlement: a homecoming for some only
strings.hist.soviet.special_settlements.text: Anyone deported during the war as a member of a people accused wholesale lived afterwards in a special settlement: obliged to report to the commandant’s office, forbidden to leave the district. A decree of 26 November 1948 declared the exile permanent; escape carried 20 years of forced labour. On 13 December 1955 the commandant’s supervision of the Soviet Germans ended – with no return to the old villages and no compensation. On 9 January 1957 the Chechens, Ingush, Kalmyks, Karachays and Balkars had their autonomy restored and were allowed home; the Crimean Tatars and Volga Germans were not. A decree of 29 August 1964 lifted the charge of treason from the Volga Germans; it was made public only in January 1965. The Crimean Tatars did not return in large numbers until 1989.
strings.hist.reich.ostarbeiter.title: “Ostarbeiter”: the special law of 1942
strings.hist.reich.ostarbeiter.text: Almost three million civilians from the occupied territories of the Soviet Union were made to do forced labour in the German Reich, more than half of them women, many still teenagers. Recruitment drives were followed by conscription and round-ups; contemporaries spoke of “manhunts”. The “Ostarbeiter decrees” of 20 February 1942 placed them under a special law: the blue-and-white “OST” badge on the chest, fenced camps, leave only to go to work, lower pay and less food, a special tax, a ban on contact with Germans. Violations meant a labour education camp or a concentration camp; intimate relations with Germans could be punished by death. Pregnant women were often forced to have abortions and newborns were taken from their mothers; tens of thousands of infants died in “foreign children’s care centres”.
strings.hist.reich.denunciation.title: Denunciation: tip-offs from the public
strings.hist.reich.denunciation.text: For a long time the Gestapo was considered all-knowing and ever-present – an image that Nazi propaganda itself had cultivated. Its files show a small authority: in Würzburg, responsible for the whole of Lower Franconia, some twenty officials worked. In 1990 Robert Gellately showed that more than half of the cases there for ‘racial defilement’ began with a denunciation from the public; in 1991 Klaus-Michael Mallmann and Gerhard Paul found much the same for the Saarland. Occasions were provided by the Treachery Act of 1934, the Nuremberg Laws, and later the ban on listening to foreign stations and the ban on contact with forced labourers. The motives were often private: quarrels between neighbours, marital conflicts, grudges. Later studies again stress the Gestapo’s own violence – yet much of what it knew, it knew only because someone told it.
